title: the things your family kept
hookLine: a medal on a keychain, a palm behind the crucifix, an abuela's altarcito: the Church's one word for all of it
last: THE SIGN OF THE CROSS · THE EUCHARIST · CONFESSION · THE ROSARY · THE SAINTS · LENT

lines: A MEDAL. A PALM. HOLY WATER.
ONE WORD FOR ALL OF IT.
cards: A Saint Christopher medal on a keychain. A palm from Palm Sunday tucked behind the crucifix, drying out for a year. A bottle of holy water in the kitchen cabinet.
An abuela's altarcito, with candles, a rosary and photos of the people she's lost. A Santo Niño, the child Jesus, watching over a Filipino living room. A medal blessed at a quinceañera Mass.
Every family's version looks different. The Church has one word for all of it.

teach.b: Sacramentals. The word is a cousin of sacrament. The seven sacraments, like baptism, confession and the Eucharist, are the big moments Catholics believe Christ himself gave the Church.
Sacramentals are the smaller things the Church added around them: blessings, blessed objects, words and gestures. Look back at this week and you'll find you've been holding them all along.
Holy water and the sign of the cross. The ashes. The rosary.
A saint's medal. The Church is careful about what they are.
They aren't magic, and they aren't lucky charms. They're reminders that help a person get ready for grace, the way a photo on the fridge reminds you to call.
Around them grows what the Church calls popular piety: the customs each people builds, which it welcomes as long as they lead back to Christ.
So a Filipino family getting up before dawn for nine Masses before Christmas, called Simbang Gabi. A Mexican family's altar for its dead in early November.
An Irish grandmother who won't eat meat on any Friday of the year. An Italian town's feast for its patron saint.
Different shapes, one faith. Whatever your family's version was, it was a way in.

how: Catholics use sacramentals such as holy water, blessed medals, rosaries, palms and ashes, ask a priest to bless homes and objects, and keep the devotions of their own families and cultures, from home altars to Simbang Gabi and patron-saint feasts.

games.q: big signs and small ones — tap the pairs.
p: a big moment Christ gave the Church
a small sign the Church added

s: the Church says they aren't magic. they're reminders that help a person get ready for grace.
holy water, ashes and rosaries are all sacramentals
blessings, blessed objects, words and gestures the Church added around the sacraments.
there's only one right way for a family to keep these customs
the Church welcomes each people's customs, as long as they lead back to Christ.

games.q: your family's customs look nothing like your friend's family's customs. in the Church's terms, which one is the real Catholic version?
o: only the one they do in Rome.
both, as long as they lead back to Christ.
games.why: popular piety: different shapes, one faith. the Church asks only that they lead back to Christ.

games.q: build the word: a cousin of sacrament.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. Bring to mind one object from your family's faith: a medal, a picture, a candle, a rosary in a drawer. On the first breath, see it.
On the second, see whose it was. On the third, let it remind you of them.

wordCard.voice: Sacramentals. Small blessed things and gestures: reminders that point to grace. Seventh word: a week's worth.

orig.note: Latin: sacramentals, things like the sacraments. the Church's word in its own law.

carryVoice: Your line: faith you can hold. That's week one: seven words, and you were already holding most of them. Tomorrow, your grandmother before dinner.
